# Unit 2: Phytochemicals as nutraceuticals and foods as functional foods

**Phytochemicals** are non-nutrient chemicals made by plants. They are not needed to prevent a deficiency disease, but many of them protect cells, lower the risk of chronic disease and are sold as nutraceuticals. This unit studies the main groups named in the syllabus — carotenoids, sulphides, polyphenolics (resveratrol), flavonoids, prebiotics and probiotics, phytoestrogens and tocopherols — and then proteins, vitamins, minerals, cereals, vegetables and beverages used as functional foods. For each group learn **where it occurs**, its **chemical nature** and its **medicinal benefits**.

```text
                       Phytochemicals
                             │
  ┌──────────────┬───────────┼────────────┬──────────────┐
Terpenoids    Phenolics   Sulphur        Fibre / sugars   Others
(carotenoids, (flavonoids, compounds     (FOS, inulin,    (probiotic
 tocopherols,  stilbenes,  (diallyl       beta-glucan)     microbes —
 saponins)     lignans,    sulphides,                      not
               isoflavones) isothiocyanates)               phytochemicals
                                                           but grouped
                                                           here)
```

## 2.1 Carotenoids

### Chemical nature

Carotenoids are **tetraterpenoids (C40)** — eight isoprene units joined into a long chain with many **conjugated double bonds**. The conjugated chain absorbs blue light, so carotenoids are **yellow, orange or red**. They are **fat-soluble**. Two groups:

| Group | Structure | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Carotenes** | Pure hydrocarbons (only C and H) | Alpha-carotene, beta-carotene, lycopene |
| **Xanthophylls** | Contain oxygen (hydroxyl, keto or epoxy groups) | Lutein, zeaxanthin, beta-cryptoxanthin, astaxanthin |

```text
Beta-carotene:  ring ─ long conjugated polyene chain ─ ring
                 (beta-ionone)      (C40)          (beta-ionone)
   cleavage in the middle → 2 molecules of retinal → vitamin A

Lycopene: open chain, no rings → cannot form vitamin A
```

### Alpha- and beta-carotene

- **Occurrence**: carrots, sweet potato, pumpkin, mango, papaya, green leafy vegetables (the green of chlorophyll hides the orange colour), red palm oil, spirulina.
- **Features**: beta-carotene has a **beta-ionone ring at both ends**; alpha-carotene has one beta- and one epsilon-ring. Both are **provitamin A** — beta-carotene gives the most vitamin A because it splits into two retinal molecules.
- **Benefits**: source of **vitamin A** (vision, epithelium, immunity) in vegetarian diets; antioxidant — quenches **singlet oxygen**; supports skin protection against light.
- **Caution**: large-dose beta-carotene supplements were linked with more lung cancer in **smokers** in clinical trials, so high-dose supplements are not advised for smokers. Food sources are safe.

### Lycopene

- **Occurrence**: **tomato** and tomato products (paste, ketchup), watermelon, pink guava, pink grapefruit, papaya.
- **Features**: **acyclic (open-chain)** carotene with 11 conjugated double bonds; red; **no provitamin A activity**; one of the **strongest singlet-oxygen quenchers** among carotenoids. In raw tomato it is mostly the all-trans form; heating with oil converts some to cis isomers and breaks the cell walls, so **cooked tomato products in oil give better absorption** than raw tomatoes.
- **Benefits**: antioxidant; studied for lower risk of **prostate cancer** and heart disease; skin protection.

### Xanthophylls — lutein and zeaxanthin

- **Occurrence**: lutein in **marigold flowers** (the commercial source), spinach, kale, other green leafy vegetables, egg yolk, maize; zeaxanthin in maize and orange peppers.
- **Features**: hydroxylated carotenoids; they are the only carotenoids concentrated in the **macula of the retina** (the "macular pigment").
- **Benefits**: filter harmful **blue light** and act as antioxidants in the eye; studied for lower risk of **age-related macular degeneration** and cataract.
- **Other xanthophylls**: beta-cryptoxanthin (oranges, papaya; provitamin A), astaxanthin (algae, salmon, shrimp — pink colour).

## 2.2 Sulphides (organosulphur compounds of Allium)

- **Occurrence**: **garlic**, onion, leek, chives (genus *Allium*).
- **Formation**: intact garlic contains **alliin**. Crushing brings it into contact with **alliinase**, giving **allicin** (diallyl thiosulphinate) within seconds. Allicin is unstable and changes into oil-soluble sulphides — **diallyl sulphide (DAS)**, **diallyl disulphide (DADS)**, **diallyl trisulphide (DATS, also called allitridin)** — and into **ajoenes** and vinyldithiins.

```text
Alliin ──alliinase (on crushing)──► Allicin ──(standing, heat, oil)──►
        Diallyl sulphide + Diallyl disulphide + Diallyl trisulphide + Ajoene
```

- **Chemical nature**: small organic molecules with two allyl groups (CH2=CH–CH2–) joined by one, two or three sulphur atoms; volatile, strong smelling, lipid-soluble.
- **Benefits**:
  - Lower total and LDL cholesterol modestly (inhibit cholesterol synthesis).
  - Reduce platelet aggregation (ajoene) — anti-thrombotic.
  - Mild lowering of blood pressure (hydrogen sulphide release relaxes blood vessels).
  - **Cancer prevention**: diallyl sulphides **modify carcinogen-metabolising enzymes** (block activation of carcinogens, induce phase II detoxification) and DATS induces apoptosis in cancer cells in experiments.
  - Antimicrobial (allicin), antioxidant.
- **Tip**: crush garlic and wait a few minutes before cooking so that allicin can form; heating whole cloves first destroys alliinase.

## 2.3 Polyphenolics — resveratrol

- **Occurrence**: skins of **red grapes**, red wine, peanuts, mulberries, blueberries; the commercial source is the root of Japanese knotweed (*Polygonum cuspidatum*).
- **Chemical nature**: a **stilbene** — **3,5,4′-trihydroxystilbene**, two phenol rings joined by an ethylene bridge. It occurs as **trans** (more active) and cis forms; plants make it as a **phytoalexin** in response to fungal attack and UV stress.
- **Benefits**:
  - Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory.
  - Cardioprotective — proposed as part of the explanation for the "**French paradox**" (low heart disease despite fatty diet, linked to red wine).
  - Activates **sirtuins (SIRT1)** and AMP-activated kinase in experiments, so it is studied for **anti-ageing** and metabolic effects.
  - Chemopreventive activity in laboratory studies.
- **Limitation**: very low oral **bioavailability** — it is rapidly conjugated in gut and liver.

## 2.4 Flavonoids

### Basic chemistry

Flavonoids are **polyphenols with a C6–C3–C6 skeleton** (two benzene rings A and B joined by a three-carbon unit that usually forms ring C, a pyran ring). Subclasses differ in ring C:

| Subclass | Ring C feature | Example in syllabus | Main source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Flavones** | 4-keto, 2,3 double bond | Apigenin, luteolin | Parsley, celery, chamomile |
| **Flavonols** | Flavone + 3-OH | **Quercetin**, kaempferol; **rutin** (quercetin glycoside) | Onion, apple, buckwheat, tea |
| **Flavanones** | 2,3 bond saturated | Naringenin; **naringin** (its glycoside), hesperidin | Grapefruit, citrus |
| **Flavan-3-ols** | No 4-keto, 3-OH | **Catechins**, EGCG | Green tea, cocoa, apples |
| **Anthocyanidins** | Flavylium cation | **Cyanidin**, delphinidin, pelargonidin | Berries, grapes, purple cabbage |
| **Isoflavones** | B ring at C-3 | Genistein, daidzein | Soya |

### Rutin

- **Occurrence**: buckwheat, citrus peel, apple, tea, *Sophora japonica* flower buds.
- **Nature**: **quercetin-3-O-rutinoside** (flavonol glycoside; rutinose = rhamnose + glucose). Also called vitamin P in old texts.
- **Benefits**: strengthens **capillaries** and reduces their fragility and leakiness (used in varicose veins, haemorrhoids, easy bruising); antioxidant; anti-inflammatory.

### Naringin

- **Occurrence**: **grapefruit** (gives its **bitter** taste), bitter orange, pomelo.
- **Nature**: **flavanone glycoside** — naringenin-7-O-neohesperidoside; gut bacteria release the aglycone **naringenin**.
- **Benefits**: antioxidant; lipid lowering in studies; used to make the sweetener neohesperidin dihydrochalcone.
- **Note**: grapefruit's **furanocoumarins** (with some contribution from naringin) **inhibit intestinal CYP3A4**, raising blood levels of drugs such as some statins and calcium-channel blockers — the classic food–drug interaction.

### Quercetin

- **Occurrence**: **onion** (red onion is rich), apples, capers, berries, tea, broccoli.
- **Nature**: **flavonol aglycone** (3,5,7,3′,4′-pentahydroxyflavone); occurs in foods mostly as glycosides.
- **Benefits**: strong antioxidant and **metal chelator**; anti-inflammatory; stabilises mast cells (anti-allergic); studied for blood pressure lowering and heart protection.

### Anthocyanidins (and anthocyanins)

- **Occurrence**: **blueberries, blackberries, black grapes, jamun, purple cabbage, red onion, black rice**, cherries.
- **Nature**: anthocyanidins are the **aglycones** (cyanidin, delphinidin, pelargonidin, malvidin, peonidin, petunidin), based on the **flavylium cation**; with sugars attached they are **anthocyanins**, the water-soluble red–blue–purple pigments. Their colour changes with **pH** (red in acid, blue/purple near neutral) and they are unstable to heat and light.
- **Benefits**: antioxidant; improve blood vessel function; studied for eye health (night vision, bilberry), memory and anti-diabetic effects; natural food colours.

### Catechins

- **Occurrence**: **green tea** (richest), black tea (partly converted to theaflavins and thearubigins during fermentation), cocoa and dark chocolate, apples, grapes.
- **Nature**: **flavan-3-ols** — catechin, epicatechin, epicatechin gallate, epigallocatechin, and **epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG)**, the main green tea catechin. Polymers form **proanthocyanidins** (condensed tannins).
- **Benefits**: antioxidant; lower LDL cholesterol; slight increase in fat burning (used in weight-management products); studied for cancer prevention; antimicrobial (oral health).
- **Caution**: concentrated green tea extracts in large amounts have been linked to liver injury.

### Flavones

- **Occurrence**: **apigenin** in parsley, celery and chamomile; **luteolin** in celery, peppers, thyme.
- **Benefits**: antioxidant, anti-inflammatory; apigenin has a mild calming effect (chamomile tea).

## 2.5 Prebiotics and probiotics

| Term | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Probiotic** | Live microorganisms which, when taken in adequate amounts, give a health benefit to the host | *Lactobacillus acidophilus*, *L. rhamnosus* GG, *L. casei*, *Bifidobacterium* species, *Saccharomyces boulardii* (yeast) |
| **Prebiotic** | Non-digestible food ingredient that is **selectively used by helpful gut bacteria** and gives a health benefit | **Fructo-oligosaccharides (FOS)**, **inulin**, galacto-oligosaccharides, lactulose, resistant starch |
| **Synbiotic** | Probiotic + prebiotic in one product | Curd with inulin |

### Fructo-oligosaccharides (FOS) and inulin

- **Occurrence**: chicory root (main commercial source of inulin), onion, garlic, banana, wheat, asparagus, Jerusalem artichoke; FOS are also made from sucrose by enzymes.
- **Chemical nature**: **fructans** — chains of fructose units joined by **β(2→1) links**, usually with a glucose at one end. FOS are short chains (about 2–10 units); inulin has longer chains. Human enzymes cannot split β(2→1) links, so they reach the colon intact.
- **Benefits**:
  - **Bifidogenic** — selectively feed bifidobacteria and lactobacilli.
  - Fermentation gives **short-chain fatty acids** (acetate, propionate, butyrate) → lower colon pH, energy for colon cells, fewer harmful bacteria.
  - Better **calcium and magnesium absorption**; relief of constipation; low-calorie sugar and fat replacer in foods.
- **Caution**: gas and bloating in large amounts.

### Lactobacillus (probiotic)

- **Nature**: Gram-positive, rod-shaped, non-spore-forming, **lactic acid bacteria**; ferment sugars to lactic acid. Found in curd, yoghurt, buttermilk, idli and dosa batter, pickles, and in the human gut and vagina.
- **Requirements for a good probiotic**: human origin or safe history, survive stomach acid and bile, stick to the gut lining, stay alive in the product until its expiry, proven benefit for the **specific strain**.
- **Mechanisms**: compete with pathogens for sites and nutrients; make lactic acid and **bacteriocins**; strengthen the gut barrier; modulate immunity.
- **Benefits**: prevention and treatment of **antibiotic-associated diarrhoea** and infective diarrhoea in children; **lactose intolerance** (bacteria supply lactase); irritable bowel syndrome; vaginal health; possibly allergy and immunity.
- Indian rules require probiotic foods to use listed strains and to contain a minimum number of live organisms per daily serving (stated on the label in colony-forming units).

## 2.6 Phytoestrogens

**Phytoestrogens** are plant compounds whose structure looks like **17β-oestradiol** (a phenol ring at a similar distance from another hydroxyl), so they bind **oestrogen receptors**, mostly **ERβ**. They act as **weak oestrogens** — and, when the body's own oestrogen is high, partly as anti-oestrogens (they behave like natural selective oestrogen receptor modulators).

| Class | Members | Sources |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Isoflavones** | **Genistein**, **daidzein**, glycitein, biochanin A, formononetin | **Soyabean** and soy foods, red clover, chickpea |
| **Lignans** | Secoisolariciresinol, matairesinol → **enterodiol, enterolactone** (mammalian lignans made by gut bacteria) | **Flaxseed** (richest), sesame, whole grains, berries |
| **Coumestans** | Coumestrol | Alfalfa and clover sprouts |

- **Daidzein** is converted by some people's gut bacteria to **equol**, which is more oestrogenic — so response to soy differs between people.
- **Benefits**: reduce **menopausal hot flushes**; slow **bone loss** after menopause; lower LDL cholesterol (soy); studied for lower risk of breast and prostate cancer (populations eating soy daily have lower rates).
- **Cautions**: concentrated supplements in women with oestrogen-sensitive cancers are used only with medical advice; may affect thyroid function when iodine intake is low.

(The syllabus prints "Geebustin" — read this as **genistein**.)

## 2.7 Tocopherols (vitamin E)

- **Chemical nature**: **vitamin E** is a family of eight compounds — four **tocopherols** (α, β, γ, δ) and four **tocotrienols**. Each has a **chromanol ring** (with the active phenolic –OH) and a 16-carbon side chain — **saturated (phytyl) in tocopherols** and **with three double bonds in tocotrienols**. The forms differ in the number and position of methyl groups on the ring.
- **α-Tocopherol** has the highest vitamin activity and is kept in the body by the liver's α-tocopherol transfer protein; natural **RRR-α-tocopherol** (d-α-tocopherol) is more active than synthetic all-rac (dl) forms. Esters (acetate, succinate) are more stable for products.
- **Occurrence**: **vegetable oils** (wheat germ oil is the richest; sunflower, safflower, rice bran, palm oil — palm and rice bran are rich in tocotrienols), nuts (almonds), seeds, green leafy vegetables.
- **Action**: the main **lipid-soluble, chain-breaking antioxidant** in membranes and lipoproteins. It gives a hydrogen atom to a lipid peroxyl radical, stopping the chain of lipid peroxidation; the resulting **tocopheroxyl radical** is stable and is recycled back by **vitamin C** (and then glutathione).
- **Benefits**: protects cell membranes and LDL from oxidation; immune function; skin; used as a **food and pharmaceutical antioxidant** (preservative for oils).
- **Deficiency** is rare (fat malabsorption, premature infants): haemolytic anaemia, neuropathy.
- **Caution**: high-dose supplements can increase bleeding tendency with anticoagulants.

## 2.8 Proteins, vitamins, minerals, cereals, vegetables and beverages as functional foods

### Proteins and peptides

- **Whey protein** — rich in branched-chain amino acids (leucine); muscle building, satiety; lactoferrin and immunoglobulins in it support immunity.
- **Casein- and whey-derived bioactive peptides** — some fermented-milk peptides inhibit ACE and lower blood pressure.
- **Soy protein** — lowers LDL cholesterol; complete plant protein.
- **Collagen peptides** — skin and joint support.

### Vitamins and minerals as functional ingredients

- **Fortified foods**: iodised salt (iodine), double-fortified salt (iron + iodine), fortified rice and wheat flour (iron, folic acid, vitamin B12), fortified milk and edible oil (vitamins A and D).
- **Antioxidant vitamins** C and E, and minerals selenium and zinc (cofactors of antioxidant enzymes).
- **Calcium + vitamin D** in fortified milk and juices for bone health.

### Cereals

| Cereal / product | Functional component | Benefit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Oats** | **Beta-glucan** (soluble fibre, β(1→3),(1→4)-glucan); avenanthramides (antioxidant) | Lowers LDL cholesterol; slows glucose rise; satiety |
| **Wheat bran** | **Insoluble fibre** (cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin), ferulic acid | Increases stool bulk, relieves constipation, lower colon cancer risk |
| **Rice bran** | **Gamma-oryzanol**, **tocotrienols**, fibre; rice bran oil | Cholesterol lowering, antioxidant |
| **Barley** | Beta-glucan | Cholesterol and glucose lowering |
| **Millets** (ragi, jowar, bajra) | Fibre, calcium (ragi), iron, polyphenols | Low glycaemic response, mineral supply |
| **Whole grains** in general | Fibre, lignans, vitamins, minerals | Lower risk of heart disease, diabetes, colon cancer |

### Vegetables and fruits

- **Tomato** — lycopene. **Carrot** — beta-carotene. **Broccoli, cabbage** — sulforaphane, indoles. **Spinach** — lutein, folate. **Onion, garlic** — quercetin, sulphides, FOS. **Beetroot** — nitrate (blood pressure), betalains. **Citrus** — vitamin C, hesperidin, naringin. **Amla** — vitamin C and tannins. **Berries, jamun** — anthocyanins.

### Sea foods

- **Fatty fish** (salmon, sardine, mackerel, Indian oil sardine) and fish oil — **omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA**: lower triglycerides, anti-inflammatory, antiplatelet, brain and eye development.
- Shellfish — glucosamine and chitosan (from shells); **seaweeds** — iodine, fucoidan, alginates (fibre); fish protein, taurine, selenium, zinc.
- Krill oil — omega-3 with astaxanthin.

### Beverages

| Beverage | Key components | Benefits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Green tea** | Catechins (EGCG), caffeine, **L-theanine** | Antioxidant, cholesterol lowering, alertness with calm (theanine) |
| **Black tea** | Theaflavins, thearubigins, caffeine | Antioxidant, vascular function |
| **Coffee** | **Caffeine**, **chlorogenic acid**, trigonelline | Alertness, antioxidant; regular coffee drinking is associated with lower risk of type 2 diabetes |
| **Cocoa** | Flavanols (epicatechin), theobromine | Improved blood vessel function, lower blood pressure |
| **Red wine / grape juice** | Resveratrol, anthocyanins, procyanidins | Antioxidant (grape juice preferred — alcohol harms) |
| **Fermented milk drinks** | Probiotics, peptides | Gut health, mild blood pressure lowering |

## Remember

- Carotenoids = C40 tetraterpenoids; carotenes (alpha, beta, lycopene) have no oxygen, xanthophylls (lutein, zeaxanthin) do. Beta-carotene → 2 retinal (provitamin A); lycopene is acyclic, no vitamin A, best singlet-oxygen quencher, better absorbed from cooked tomato in oil; lutein and zeaxanthin protect the macula.
- Garlic: alliin → (alliinase) allicin → diallyl sulphide, disulphide, trisulphide (allitridin), ajoene — cholesterol, platelets, cancer prevention.
- Resveratrol = 3,5,4′-trihydroxystilbene, red grape skin, phytoalexin, SIRT1, French paradox, poor bioavailability.
- Flavonoids C6–C3–C6: rutin (quercetin rutinoside, capillaries), naringin (grapefruit flavanone glycoside, bitter), quercetin (onion flavonol), anthocyanidins (berries, flavylium, pH colour), catechins (green tea EGCG), flavones (apigenin, luteolin).
- FOS and inulin = β(2→1) fructans, bifidogenic, short-chain fatty acids; *Lactobacillus* = lactic acid bacteria, strain-specific benefit.
- Phytoestrogens: isoflavones (genistein, daidzein → equol), lignans (flax SDG → enterolactone), coumestans; weak ERβ agonists.
- Vitamin E: 4 tocopherols + 4 tocotrienols, chromanol ring, α-tocopherol most active, chain-breaking antioxidant recycled by vitamin C.
- Functional foods: oats beta-glucan, wheat bran insoluble fibre, rice bran oryzanol, fish omega-3, tea catechins and theanine, coffee chlorogenic acid.

# Unit 3: Free radicals, and dietary fibre as a functional food ingredient

The first half of this unit explains what free radicals are, how cells make them, and how they damage the four big classes of biomolecules — lipids, proteins, carbohydrates and nucleic acids. This is the base for Unit 4 (free radicals in disease, and antioxidants). The second half covers dietary fibre and complex carbohydrates, the most widely used functional food ingredients.

## 3.1 Free radicals — definitions

A **free radical** is **any atom or molecule that has one or more unpaired electrons** in its outer orbital and can exist on its own. The unpaired electron is shown by a dot (•). Because electrons are stable only in pairs, a radical is **highly reactive**: it takes an electron from (oxidises) or gives an electron to (reduces) a nearby molecule, or adds to it. The molecule that loses an electron often becomes a radical itself, so radicals start **chain reactions**.

Radicals form in three ways:

1. **Homolytic cleavage** of a covalent bond — each fragment keeps one electron (A:B → A• + B•); caused by heat, UV light, ionising radiation.
2. **Loss of one electron** from a normal molecule (oxidation).
3. **Gain of one electron** by a normal molecule (reduction) — for example O2 + e⁻ → O2•⁻.

### Reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS)

"Reactive oxygen species" is a wider term: it includes oxygen radicals **and** reactive non-radical oxygen compounds.

| Species | Symbol | Radical? | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Superoxide anion | O2•⁻ | Yes | First product of one-electron reduction of oxygen; made by mitochondria and NADPH oxidase |
| Hydroxyl radical | •OH | Yes | **Most reactive** and most damaging; reacts with almost anything at the site where it forms |
| Hydroperoxyl radical | HO2• | Yes | Protonated superoxide; more lipid-soluble |
| Peroxyl radical | ROO• | Yes | Carries on lipid peroxidation |
| Alkoxyl radical | RO• | Yes | From breakdown of lipid hydroperoxides |
| Hydrogen peroxide | H2O2 | **No** | Crosses membranes; gives •OH with iron (Fenton reaction) |
| Singlet oxygen | ¹O2 | **No** | Excited oxygen made by light with photosensitisers; quenched by carotenoids |
| Hypochlorous acid | HOCl | **No** | Made by myeloperoxidase in neutrophils |
| Ozone | O3 | **No** | Air pollutant |
| Nitric oxide | NO• | Yes (RNS) | Signal molecule, vasodilator |
| Peroxynitrite | ONOO⁻ | **No** (RNS) | NO• + O2•⁻; strong oxidant and nitrating agent |

**Oxidative stress** is the condition in which the production of ROS/RNS is **greater than the antioxidant defences** can handle, leading to damage of biomolecules. At low levels, ROS are **useful**: they kill microbes in phagocytes and act as signalling molecules (redox signalling). Problems arise only when the balance tips.

```text
       Oxidants (ROS, RNS)              Antioxidants
 ┌──────────────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────────┐
 │ mitochondria, NADPH oxid, │ vs │ SOD, catalase, GPx,     │
 │ xanthine oxidase, CYP450, │    │ glutathione, vit C, E,  │
 │ pollution, smoke, UV      │    │ carotenoids, flavonoids │
 └──────────────────────────┘    └─────────────────────────┘
        oxidants > defences  →  OXIDATIVE STRESS → damage
```

## 3.2 Production of free radicals in cells

### A. Internal (endogenous) sources

1. **Mitochondrial electron transport chain** — the largest source. During normal respiration, a small fraction of electrons **leak** from complexes I and III and reduce oxygen to **superoxide** instead of passing to complex IV (where oxygen is fully reduced to water).
2. **NADPH oxidase (NOX)** in neutrophils and macrophages — makes large amounts of superoxide deliberately during the **respiratory burst** to kill engulfed microbes; **myeloperoxidase** then makes HOCl from H2O2 and chloride.
3. **Xanthine oxidase** — oxidises hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid and reduces oxygen to superoxide and H2O2; very important in **ischaemia–reperfusion injury** (Unit 4).
4. **Cytochrome P450 enzymes** in the endoplasmic reticulum — leak superoxide while metabolising drugs and toxins; some drugs and toxins (carbon tetrachloride, paracetamol overdose) are converted to radicals or reactive metabolites.
5. **Peroxisomes** — fatty-acid oxidation produces H2O2.
6. **Nitric oxide synthase** — makes NO•, which with superoxide forms peroxynitrite.
7. **Auto-oxidation** of small molecules — catecholamines, flavins, haemoglobin (forming methaemoglobin and superoxide).
8. **Transition metals** — free **iron (Fe²⁺)** and **copper (Cu⁺)** turn H2O2 into the hydroxyl radical.

### Key reactions

```text
One-electron reduction of oxygen (step by step):
 O2 ──e⁻──► O2•⁻ ──e⁻ + 2H⁺──► H2O2 ──e⁻──► •OH + OH⁻ ──e⁻ + H⁺──► H2O

Fenton reaction:
 Fe²⁺ + H2O2 → Fe³⁺ + •OH + OH⁻

Haber–Weiss reaction (iron-catalysed overall):
 O2•⁻ + H2O2 → O2 + •OH + OH⁻
 (superoxide recycles Fe³⁺ back to Fe²⁺: O2•⁻ + Fe³⁺ → O2 + Fe²⁺)

Peroxynitrite formation:
 NO• + O2•⁻ → ONOO⁻
```

### B. External (exogenous) sources

- **Ionising radiation** (X-rays, gamma rays) splits water → •OH (radiolysis); **UV light** on skin.
- **Cigarette smoke** — very rich in radicals in both tar and gas phases.
- **Air pollution** — ozone, nitrogen dioxide, particulate matter.
- **Drugs and chemicals** — paracetamol overdose, doxorubicin (redox cycling of its quinone), bleomycin, paraquat, carbon tetrachloride, alcohol (via CYP2E1).
- **Heavy metals** — iron overload, copper, cadmium, lead, mercury.
- **Diet** — oxidised and repeatedly heated frying oils, excess iron, alcohol.
- Strenuous exercise and infection temporarily raise ROS.

## 3.3 Damaging reactions of free radicals

### A. Lipids — lipid peroxidation

**Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs)** in membranes are the most easily attacked, because the **methylene (–CH2–) group between two double bonds** has weak C–H bonds. Lipid peroxidation is a **chain reaction** with three stages:

```text
1. INITIATION
   LH (PUFA) + •OH  →  L• (lipid radical) + H2O
   (hydrogen taken from the bis-allylic CH2; the double bonds shift to a conjugated diene)

2. PROPAGATION (repeats again and again)
   L•  + O2   →  LOO•  (lipid peroxyl radical)
   LOO• + LH  →  LOOH (lipid hydroperoxide) + L•   ← new radical keeps the chain going

3. TERMINATION
   LOO• + LOO•  →  non-radical products
   LOO• + vitamin E (TOH)  →  LOOH + TO• (stable tocopheroxyl radical)  ← chain-breaking antioxidant
```

- Lipid hydroperoxides break down (helped by iron) into **alkoxyl radicals** and into **aldehydes** such as **malondialdehyde (MDA)** and **4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE)**, which are toxic and cross-link proteins and DNA.
- **Consequences**: membranes become stiff and leaky, membrane enzymes and receptors fail, ion pumps stop working, organelles burst, the cell may die. **Oxidised LDL** is taken up by macrophages to form foam cells in atherosclerosis. In foods, the same process makes fats **rancid**.
- **Markers**: MDA measured as **thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS)**; **F2-isoprostanes** (from arachidonic acid; considered reliable markers); conjugated dienes; 4-HNE adducts.

### B. Proteins

- **Oxidation of amino acid side chains** — **cysteine** (thiol → disulphide, sulphenic and higher acids) and **methionine** (→ methionine sulphoxide) are most sensitive; aromatic amino acids (tyrosine, tryptophan, histidine) are also attacked.
- **Protein carbonyl formation** — oxidation of lysine, arginine, proline and threonine gives carbonyl groups; **protein carbonyls** are the most used marker of protein oxidation.
- **Nitration** of tyrosine by peroxynitrite → **3-nitrotyrosine**.
- **Cross-linking** (dityrosine bridges, links through MDA and 4-HNE) and **fragmentation** of the backbone.
- **Consequences**: loss of enzyme activity, unfolding and **aggregation**, faster breakdown by the proteasome, damaged receptors and transporters, new antigens (autoimmunity). Oxidised, cross-linked lens proteins contribute to **cataract**.

### C. Carbohydrates

- **Glycoxidation**: reducing sugars such as glucose react with protein amino groups (Maillard reaction → Schiff base → Amadori product). With oxidation, these form **advanced glycation end products (AGEs)** such as carboxymethyl-lysine and pentosidine; the process also releases more ROS. AGEs stiffen collagen and blood vessels and act on the **RAGE** receptor to cause inflammation — important in **diabetic complications** and ageing.
- **Auto-oxidation of glucose** in high-glucose states produces superoxide, H2O2 and reactive dicarbonyls (glyoxal, methylglyoxal).
- **Depolymerisation of polysaccharides** — •OH breaks **hyaluronic acid** in joint fluid, lowering its viscosity (seen in inflammatory arthritis).
- The **deoxyribose** sugar of DNA is attacked, causing strand breaks.

### D. Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA)

- **Base modification** — the hydroxyl radical adds to bases. The best-known product is **8-oxo-7,8-dihydro-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-oxo-dG, also 8-OHdG)**; it pairs wrongly with adenine, causing **G:C → T:A transversion mutations**. 8-oxo-dG in urine is a marker of oxidative DNA damage.
- **Sugar damage and strand breaks** — single- and double-strand breaks.
- **Abasic sites** — loss of a base.
- **DNA–protein cross-links**; MDA forms DNA adducts.
- **Mitochondrial DNA** is especially exposed (close to the electron transport chain, no histones, less repair).
- **Consequences**: mutation → **cancer**; cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis; ageing. The cell repairs much of this damage (base excision repair).

### Summary table

| Target | Main damage | Marker | Disease link |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lipids | Peroxidation chain reaction | MDA (TBARS), F2-isoprostanes, 4-HNE | Atherosclerosis, membrane injury |
| Proteins | Carbonyls, thiol oxidation, nitration, cross-links | Protein carbonyls, 3-nitrotyrosine | Cataract, neurodegeneration, ageing |
| Carbohydrates | Glycoxidation, AGEs, polysaccharide breakdown | AGEs (CML, pentosidine) | Diabetic complications, arthritis |
| Nucleic acids | Base oxidation, strand breaks | 8-oxo-dG | Cancer, ageing |

## 3.4 Dietary fibre and complex carbohydrates as functional food ingredients

### Definitions

- **Complex carbohydrates** are carbohydrates made of many sugar units — **starch** (digestible) and **non-starch polysaccharides** (mostly indigestible) — as against simple sugars.
- **Dietary fibre** is the **edible part of plants and analogous carbohydrates that resists digestion and absorption in the human small intestine**, with complete or partial **fermentation in the large intestine**. It includes polysaccharides, oligosaccharides, lignin and associated plant substances.
- **Resistant starch** is starch that escapes digestion in the small intestine (in unripe banana, cooled cooked rice and potatoes, legumes) and behaves like fibre.

### Classification by solubility

| Property | **Soluble fibre** | **Insoluble fibre** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Behaviour in water | Dissolves or swells to form a **viscous gel** | Does not dissolve; holds water, adds bulk |
| Examples | **Pectin** (apple, citrus), **beta-glucan** (oats, barley), **gums** (guar, gum arabic), **mucilages** (psyllium/isabgol), **inulin, FOS**, alginate, glucomannan | **Cellulose**, **hemicellulose** (most types), **lignin** (non-carbohydrate), resistant starch (part) |
| Sources | Oats, barley, legumes, fruits, isabgol husk, flax | Wheat bran, whole grains, vegetable skins, nuts |
| Fermentation in colon | **Highly fermented** → short-chain fatty acids | Poorly fermented |
| Main effects | Lowers **LDL cholesterol**, slows **glucose** rise, satiety, prebiotic | Increases **stool bulk**, speeds **transit**, relieves **constipation** |

### Physiological effects and how they work

1. **Cholesterol lowering** (soluble, viscous fibres) — bind **bile acids** in the gut and increase their loss in faeces; the liver uses more cholesterol to make new bile acids, so blood LDL falls. Short-chain fatty acid **propionate** may also reduce cholesterol synthesis.
2. **Blood glucose control** — viscous gel slows **gastric emptying** and the contact of starch with enzymes, flattening the post-meal glucose and insulin peaks (lower **glycaemic index** of the meal). Useful in diabetes.
3. **Weight control** — fibre-rich foods are bulky and low in energy, need more chewing, and increase **satiety**.
4. **Bowel function** — insoluble fibre and psyllium increase stool weight and water, soften stools and speed transit; relief of **constipation**, **haemorrhoids** and **diverticular disease**; lower risk of **colon cancer** (dilution and faster removal of carcinogens, butyrate effects).
5. **Prebiotic effect** — fermentation by colonic bacteria produces **short-chain fatty acids** (**acetate, propionate, butyrate**). **Butyrate** is the main fuel of colon cells and has anti-inflammatory and anti-cancer actions; the colon pH falls, discouraging pathogens; mineral absorption (calcium) improves.
6. **Blood pressure** — whole-grain, high-fibre diets are associated with lower blood pressure.

### Fibres used as functional food ingredients

| Ingredient | Source | Use in foods |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Psyllium (isabgol) husk** | *Plantago ovata* seed husk | Bulk laxative, cholesterol lowering, fibre drinks |
| **Oat and barley beta-glucan** | Oats, barley | Breakfast cereals, bars; cholesterol lowering |
| **Pectin** | Citrus peel, apple pomace | Gelling agent in jams, cholesterol lowering |
| **Guar gum** | *Cyamopsis tetragonoloba* seed (galactomannan) | Thickener, glucose control |
| **Inulin and FOS** | Chicory root | Prebiotic, fat and sugar replacer |
| **Resistant starch / resistant dextrin** | Maize, tapioca, modified starch | Added fibre in breads, drinks |
| **Wheat bran** | Wheat | Breakfast cereals, high-fibre bread |
| **Glucomannan** | Konjac tuber | Weight-loss products (fullness) |
| **Cellulose derivatives** | Wood pulp, cotton | Bulking, texture |

### Possible problems with high fibre

- **Gas, bloating** and abdominal discomfort if fibre is increased too quickly — increase slowly and drink enough water.
- Bulk fibres taken with little water can cause **choking or intestinal obstruction**.
- Very high intakes of phytate-rich bran can reduce absorption of **iron, zinc, calcium**.
- Fibre supplements can **reduce absorption of some drugs** taken at the same time — leave a gap between the fibre and medicines.

## Remember

- Free radical = species with one or more unpaired electrons; ROS include radicals (O2•⁻, •OH, ROO•) and non-radicals (H2O2, ¹O2, HOCl); •OH is the most reactive.
- Oxidative stress = oxidants exceed antioxidant defences.
- Sources: mitochondrial leak (largest), NADPH oxidase respiratory burst, xanthine oxidase, CYP450, peroxisomes, Fenton reaction (Fe²⁺ + H2O2 → •OH); external — radiation, smoke, pollution, drugs, metals.
- Lipid peroxidation: initiation, propagation (L• + O2 → LOO•; LOO• + LH → LOOH + L•), termination by vitamin E; markers MDA (TBARS), F2-isoprostanes.
- Proteins: carbonyls, thiol oxidation, 3-nitrotyrosine, cross-links. Carbohydrates: AGEs, hyaluronic acid breakdown. DNA: 8-oxo-dG (G→T mutations), strand breaks.
- Dietary fibre resists digestion in the small intestine and is fermented in the colon. Soluble (pectin, beta-glucan, gums, psyllium, inulin) → lowers LDL and glucose; insoluble (cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin) → bulk and transit.
- Fermentation gives acetate, propionate, butyrate (butyrate fuels colon cells).

# Unit 4: Free radicals in disease, antioxidants and functional foods for chronic disease

Unit 3 showed how free radicals form and what they damage. This unit applies that knowledge to **diseases** — diabetes, inflammation, ischaemia–reperfusion injury, cancer, atherosclerosis, brain disorders, kidney and muscle damage — and to **ageing**. It then describes the body's **antioxidant defences** (enzymes and small molecules), two **synthetic antioxidants** used in foods (BHT, BHA), and finally the **functional foods** used to prevent chronic disease.

A good long answer on any disease in this unit follows the same plan:

```text
Where do extra ROS come from?  →  What do they damage?  →  What is the result?
→  Evidence (markers)  →  Antioxidant / dietary approach
```

## 4.1 Free radicals in diabetes mellitus

**Sources of extra ROS in high blood glucose (hyperglycaemia):**

1. **Glucose auto-oxidation** — glucose and its products oxidise in the presence of metals, forming superoxide, H2O2 and reactive dicarbonyls.
2. **Advanced glycation end products (AGEs)** — formed by non-enzymatic glycation of proteins plus oxidation; AGEs binding to their receptor **RAGE** switch on NADPH oxidase and inflammatory signalling (NF-κB).
3. **Polyol (sorbitol) pathway** — aldose reductase turns excess glucose into sorbitol using **NADPH**; less NADPH means less regeneration of reduced **glutathione**, so antioxidant defence falls.
4. **Protein kinase C activation** (through diacylglycerol) increases NADPH oxidase activity.
5. **Hexosamine pathway** — altered gene expression and inflammation.
6. **Mitochondrial overproduction of superoxide** — thought to link all four pathways above.

**Effects:**

- **β-cells** of the pancreas have **low levels of antioxidant enzymes** (catalase, glutathione peroxidase), so they are easily damaged by ROS → reduced insulin secretion. Experimental diabetes is produced in animals with **alloxan** and **streptozotocin**, which destroy β-cells partly through ROS.
- ROS interfere with insulin signalling → **insulin resistance**.
- **Complications**: endothelial damage → **micro-vascular** (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and **macro-vascular** disease (coronary, stroke); cataract (oxidised lens proteins); poor wound healing.

**Evidence**: higher MDA, AGEs and protein carbonyls; lower glutathione and vitamin C in diabetic patients.

**Diet**: good glucose control is the main step. **Alpha-lipoic acid** is used in some countries for diabetic neuropathy; fibre-rich diets, polyphenol-rich foods and omega-3 support overall control.

## 4.2 Free radicals in inflammation

- At a site of infection or injury, **neutrophils and macrophages** gather and switch on **NADPH oxidase** (the **respiratory burst**), producing superoxide; **myeloperoxidase** converts H2O2 and chloride into **hypochlorous acid (HOCl)**; inducible nitric oxide synthase makes NO•, which forms **peroxynitrite** with superoxide.
- These oxidants **kill microbes** — useful — but in **chronic inflammation** they spill out and damage the host's own tissue.
- ROS activate the transcription factor **NF-κB**, increasing inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6), COX-2 and adhesion molecules — so inflammation and oxidative stress **feed each other** (a vicious circle).
- Examples: **rheumatoid arthritis** (•OH breaks down hyaluronic acid in synovial fluid, cartilage damage), **inflammatory bowel disease**, asthma, chronic hepatitis, periodontitis.
- **Dietary help**: omega-3 fatty acids (anti-inflammatory mediators), curcumin, flavonoids (quercetin), vitamin C and E.

## 4.3 Ischaemia–reperfusion injury

**Ischaemia** is the loss of blood supply to a tissue; **reperfusion** is the return of blood (for example after clot-busting treatment or angioplasty in a heart attack, organ transplantation, or after surgery). Paradoxically, **much of the damage happens when oxygen returns**.

```text
ISCHAEMIA (no oxygen)
 ATP → ADP → AMP → adenosine → inosine → HYPOXANTHINE accumulates
 Ca²⁺ rises in cell → protease converts xanthine DEHYDROGENASE
                       into xanthine OXIDASE
                    │
REPERFUSION (oxygen returns suddenly)
 Hypoxanthine + O2 ──xanthine oxidase──► xanthine + O2•⁻ + H2O2
 Xanthine + O2   ──xanthine oxidase──► uric acid + O2•⁻ + H2O2
                    │
 O2•⁻ + H2O2 + Fe²⁺ (Fenton) → •OH
 + damaged mitochondria leak more superoxide
 + neutrophils arrive → respiratory burst
                    │
 Lipid peroxidation, protein and DNA damage, Ca²⁺ overload,
 opening of mitochondrial pores → cell death (myocardial stunning,
 arrhythmias, graft failure)
```

- Seen in **heart** (myocardial infarction treatment), **brain** (stroke), **kidney** and **liver** transplants, intestine.
- Protective approaches studied: **allopurinol** (xanthine oxidase inhibitor), antioxidants, iron chelators, and organ-preservation solutions containing glutathione and allopurinol; **ischaemic preconditioning** (short ischaemic episodes before a long one).

## 4.4 Free radicals in cancer

Free radicals take part in all three stages of carcinogenesis:

| Stage | Role of ROS |
| --- | --- |
| **Initiation** | Oxidative **DNA damage** (8-oxo-dG, strand breaks) → **mutations** in oncogenes (*ras*) and tumour-suppressor genes (*p53*) |
| **Promotion** | ROS act as signals that increase cell growth (activation of NF-κB, AP-1, MAP kinases); tumour promoters such as phorbol esters raise ROS |
| **Progression** | Genetic instability, angiogenesis, invasion and metastasis |

- **Chronic inflammation** drives cancer through ROS: *Helicobacter pylori* gastritis → stomach cancer; hepatitis B and C → liver cancer; ulcerative colitis → colon cancer.
- Carcinogens such as tobacco smoke, asbestos and ionising radiation act partly through radicals.
- **Two sides**: cancer cells often have high ROS, and many **anticancer drugs and radiotherapy** kill cells by generating ROS (doxorubicin, bleomycin). So high-dose antioxidant supplements during chemotherapy or radiotherapy are not routinely advised.
- **Dietary prevention**: fruits and vegetables rich in antioxidants and phytochemicals (lycopene, sulforaphane, EGCG, curcumin, resveratrol), fibre, and avoiding tobacco and alcohol. Large trials of single antioxidant supplements have not shown clear cancer prevention, and beta-carotene raised lung cancer risk in smokers — whole foods are preferred.

## 4.5 Free radicals in atherosclerosis

The **oxidative modification hypothesis**:

```text
LDL enters the artery wall (intima)
        │  ROS from endothelium, macrophages, smooth muscle
        ▼
Oxidised LDL (ox-LDL): lipid peroxidation + modified apoB-100
        │
 • Taken up by macrophage SCAVENGER receptors (not down-regulated)
   → cholesterol-loaded FOAM CELLS → FATTY STREAK
 • Damages endothelium, reduces nitric oxide (endothelial dysfunction)
 • Attracts more monocytes (chemotactic), causes inflammation
 • Stimulates smooth-muscle growth → fibrous PLAQUE
        │
 Plaque rupture → thrombosis → heart attack, stroke
```

- **Risk factors** that increase ROS: smoking, diabetes, hypertension (angiotensin II activates NADPH oxidase), high LDL, obesity.
- Superoxide destroys **nitric oxide**, the vessel-relaxing and anti-platelet molecule.
- **Protection by diet**: polyphenols (tea, cocoa, red grapes), vitamin E within LDL, omega-3 fatty acids, soluble fibre and plant sterols (lower LDL), garlic, a Mediterranean-type diet.

## 4.6 Free radicals in brain metabolism and pathology

**Why the brain is very vulnerable:**

1. Uses a **large share of the body's oxygen** for its small weight → much mitochondrial ROS.
2. Rich in **PUFAs** (DHA, arachidonic acid) — easily peroxidised.
3. Contains **iron** in several regions (iron can drive the Fenton reaction).
4. Relatively **low catalase** and modest glutathione peroxidase activity.
5. **Auto-oxidation of dopamine** and its metabolism by **MAO** produce H2O2 and quinones.
6. **Excitotoxicity** — excess glutamate → Ca²⁺ influx → nitric oxide synthase and mitochondrial ROS.
7. Neurons hardly divide, so damage builds up.

**Diseases:**

| Disease | Role of ROS |
| --- | --- |
| **Parkinson's disease** | Dopamine oxidation and MAO-B → H2O2; iron in substantia nigra; complex I defect; lower glutathione; toxins (MPTP → MPP⁺) act through mitochondrial ROS |
| **Alzheimer's disease** | Beta-amyloid with copper and iron produces H2O2 and lipid peroxidation; protein oxidation; mitochondrial dysfunction |
| **Stroke** | Ischaemia–reperfusion and excitotoxicity |
| **Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis** | Some familial cases are caused by mutations in **Cu/Zn-SOD (SOD1)** |
| Others | Huntington's disease, epilepsy, brain trauma |

## 4.7 Free radicals in kidney and muscle damage, and other disorders

**Kidney damage**:

- **Drug nephrotoxicity** — cisplatin, aminoglycosides (gentamicin), ciclosporin and radiocontrast agents act partly through ROS.
- **Ischaemia–reperfusion** in renal transplants and shock.
- **Diabetic nephropathy** and glomerulonephritis (neutrophils, AGEs).
- **Rhabdomyolysis** — myoglobin released from damaged muscle; its haem iron catalyses lipid peroxidation in kidney tubules → acute kidney injury.

**Muscle damage**:

- **Strenuous or unaccustomed exercise** raises oxygen use and ROS → muscle soreness, fatigue and damage (markers such as creatine kinase rise). Moderate regular exercise, in contrast, **increases** the body's antioxidant enzymes (adaptation).
- **Muscular dystrophies**, **ischaemia–reperfusion** of limbs, and ageing (sarcopenia).
- **Vitamin E and selenium deficiency** cause muscle disease in animals (white muscle disease).

**Other disorders involving free radicals**:

- **Eye**: cataract (lens protein oxidation), **age-related macular degeneration**, retinopathy of prematurity (high oxygen in premature babies).
- **Lungs**: smoking-related **COPD**, asthma, **acute respiratory distress syndrome**, oxygen toxicity, paraquat poisoning.
- **Liver**: alcoholic liver disease (CYP2E1), paracetamol overdose, carbon tetrachloride, iron overload.
- **Skin**: UV damage, photo-ageing, skin cancer.
- **Blood**: haemolysis in **G6PD deficiency** (low NADPH → low glutathione), thalassaemia with iron overload.
- **Infection** — HIV, malaria (red cell oxidative damage).

## 4.8 Free radical theory of ageing

Proposed by **Denham Harman in 1956**, the theory states that **ageing results from the gradual, lifelong build-up of damage to cells and tissues caused by free radicals** made during normal metabolism.

**Supporting points:**

- Oxidative damage to DNA, proteins (carbonyls) and lipids **increases with age**; the age pigment **lipofuscin** (oxidised lipid–protein material) builds up in neurons and heart muscle.
- Animal species with **higher metabolic rates** and more ROS production tend to live shorter lives (link with the older "rate of living" theory).
- **Caloric restriction**, which lowers ROS production, extends lifespan in many laboratory animals.
- **Mitochondrial theory** (an extension): mitochondrial DNA is damaged by ROS → faulty respiratory chain → still more ROS — a vicious circle.

**Limitations:**

- Antioxidant supplements have **not extended lifespan** in human trials.
- Some long-lived animals (for example naked mole-rats) have high oxidative damage.
- ROS are also useful signals; ageing is now seen as having many causes (telomere shortening, protein misfolding, inflammation, genetic programmes), with oxidative damage one contributor.

## 4.9 Antioxidants

An **antioxidant** is **any substance that, at low concentration compared with an oxidisable substrate, significantly delays or prevents the oxidation of that substrate** (a definition given by Halliwell).

### Ways antioxidants act

| Type | Action | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Preventive** | Stop radicals forming — remove peroxides, bind metals | Catalase, glutathione peroxidase, transferrin, ferritin, ceruloplasmin, albumin |
| **Radical scavenging / chain-breaking** | React with radicals and stop the chain | Vitamin E, vitamin C, carotenoids, uric acid, flavonoids, BHT, BHA |
| **Repair** | Remove and replace damaged molecules | DNA repair enzymes, proteasomes, methionine sulphoxide reductase |
| **Adaptation** | Increase antioxidant enzymes when stressed | Nrf2 pathway (switched on by sulforaphane) |

### A. Endogenous enzymatic antioxidants

```text
             O2•⁻
              │  SOD
              ▼
             H2O2 ──── catalase ────► H2O + O2
              │
              └── glutathione peroxidase (Se) ──► H2O
                     2 GSH  →  GSSG
                                │ glutathione reductase
                                │ (NADPH from pentose phosphate pathway)
                                ▼
                              2 GSH
```

**Superoxide dismutase (SOD)**

- Reaction: **2 O2•⁻ + 2 H⁺ → H2O2 + O2** (dismutation — one superoxide is oxidised, the other reduced).
- Forms: **Cu/Zn-SOD (SOD1)** in the cytosol; **Mn-SOD (SOD2)** in mitochondria (essential for life in animals); **extracellular SOD (SOD3, Cu/Zn)** in tissue fluids and vessel walls.
- The **first line of defence** against superoxide; it must work together with catalase or peroxidases, because its product H2O2 is still harmful.

**Catalase**

- Reaction: **2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2**.
- A **haem (iron-porphyrin)** enzyme found mainly in **peroxisomes**; very high in liver and red blood cells, low in the brain and pancreatic β-cells.
- Handles **high concentrations** of H2O2; one of the fastest enzymes known.

**Glutathione peroxidase (GPx)**

- Reaction: **H2O2 + 2 GSH → GSSG + 2 H2O**, and **ROOH + 2 GSH → ROH + GSSG + H2O** — it also reduces **lipid hydroperoxides**.
- A **selenium-containing enzyme** (selenocysteine at its active site) — this is why **selenium** is an antioxidant nutrient.
- Removes **low levels** of H2O2 all the time, in cytosol and mitochondria.
- Works with **glutathione reductase** (a FAD enzyme that uses NADPH) to regenerate GSH. Other helpers: glutathione S-transferases, peroxiredoxins and thioredoxin.

### B. Endogenous non-enzymatic antioxidants

**Glutathione (GSH)**

- **Tripeptide γ-glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine**; its active part is the **thiol (–SH) of cysteine**; the γ-link makes it resistant to ordinary peptidases. Made in all cells, with high levels in the liver.
- Functions: substrate of **GPx**; directly scavenges •OH and singlet oxygen; regenerates **vitamins C and E**; keeps protein thiols reduced; conjugates drugs and toxins (**glutathione S-transferases**) — e.g. it detoxifies the reactive metabolite of paracetamol (**N-acetylcysteine** is used in paracetamol poisoning to restore GSH).
- The **GSH : GSSG ratio** is a key index of the cell's redox state.

**Alpha-lipoic acid**

- An **8-carbon fatty acid with a dithiolane ring** (two sulphur atoms); made in mitochondria and found in meat (organ meats), spinach, broccoli.
- Normally a **cofactor** of **pyruvate dehydrogenase** and **α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase**.
- Its reduced form, **dihydrolipoic acid (DHLA)**, and the oxidised form together make a strong **redox couple**: they scavenge several ROS, **chelate metals**, and **regenerate** other antioxidants — **vitamin C, vitamin E (via vitamin C), glutathione** and coenzyme Q10 — so lipoic acid is called the "**antioxidant of antioxidants**" or a network antioxidant.
- Soluble in **both water and fat**, so it acts in cytosol and membranes.
- Studied and used for **diabetic neuropathy**, insulin sensitivity.

**Melatonin**

- **N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine**, an **indoleamine** made from **tryptophan** (via serotonin) mainly by the **pineal gland** at night; also in the gut and in some foods.
- **Amphiphilic** — crosses membranes and the **blood–brain barrier** easily.
- Directly scavenges **•OH**, peroxynitrite and other radicals; its breakdown products are themselves antioxidants (a cascade); **increases** the activity of SOD, catalase and GPx; does not cause redox cycling (does not become a pro-oxidant).
- Better known for sleep and circadian rhythm; production falls with age.

**Other endogenous small molecules**: **uric acid** (a major plasma antioxidant), **bilirubin**, **coenzyme Q10** (ubiquinol in membranes), **albumin** (thiol groups), metal-binding proteins **transferrin, ferritin, ceruloplasmin, lactoferrin, metallothionein**.

### C. Dietary (exogenous) antioxidants

Vitamin C (water-phase scavenger, recycles vitamin E), vitamin E (lipid-phase chain-breaker), carotenoids (singlet oxygen quenchers), flavonoids and other polyphenols, selenium and zinc (enzyme cofactors), copper and manganese (SOD cofactors).

### D. Synthetic antioxidants

**Butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT)** and **butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA)** are **hindered phenols** added to fats, oils, fat-containing foods, cosmetics, and pharmaceutical products (vitamin A and E preparations, oily injections, ointments) to **prevent rancidity**.

| Feature | **BHT** | **BHA** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chemical name | 2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol | Mixture of 2- and 3-tert-butyl-4-hydroxyanisole (methoxyphenol) |
| Structure | Phenol with **two** bulky tert-butyl groups beside the –OH | Phenol with **one** tert-butyl group and a methoxy group |
| Solubility | Fat-soluble, insoluble in water | Fat-soluble, insoluble in water |
| Heat stability ("carry-through" in baking and frying) | Moderate; somewhat volatile | Good in animal fats and baked goods |

**Mechanism** — chain-breaking: the phenolic –OH gives a **hydrogen atom** to a lipid peroxyl radical (LOO•), forming LOOH and a **phenoxyl radical**. The bulky tert-butyl groups and the ring **stabilise** this radical (resonance and steric hindrance) so it cannot continue the chain:

```text
LOO•  +  ArOH (BHT/BHA)  →  LOOH  +  ArO•  (stable, unreactive)
ArO•  +  LOO•            →  non-radical products
```

- They work **synergistically** with each other and with **citric acid** (metal chelator) and ascorbyl palmitate.
- Other synthetic food antioxidants: **propyl gallate**, **tert-butylhydroquinone (TBHQ)**; ascorbyl palmitate (semi-synthetic).
- **Safety**: permitted only within limits set by food regulations; their safety has been debated, so there is a trend to replace them with natural antioxidants (tocopherols, rosemary extract).

### Antioxidant network and the pro-oxidant problem

```text
 LOO• ──► vitamin E ──► tocopheroxyl radical
                         │ recycled by
                         ▼
                    vitamin C ──► ascorbyl radical
                         │ recycled by
                         ▼
                    glutathione / lipoic acid ──► GSSG
                         │ recycled by
                         ▼
                 glutathione reductase + NADPH
```

Antioxidants protect best as a **team**. A single antioxidant at high dose, in the presence of free iron or copper, can act as a **pro-oxidant** (for example, vitamin C reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺, feeding the Fenton reaction). This is one reason why mixed antioxidants from foods are preferred to mega-dose single supplements.

## 4.10 Functional foods for chronic disease prevention

| Chronic disease | Functional foods and their active components |
| --- | --- |
| **Coronary heart disease** | Oats and barley (beta-glucan), plant sterol/stanol-enriched foods, soy protein, nuts (almonds, walnuts), fatty fish (EPA, DHA), flaxseed (ALA, lignans), green and black tea, cocoa (flavanols), garlic, olive oil (oleic acid, polyphenols), red grapes |
| **Hypertension** | Fruits and vegetables rich in potassium, low-fat dairy and fermented milk peptides, beetroot (nitrate), cocoa, garlic, low-salt foods (DASH-type diet) |
| **Type 2 diabetes** | Whole grains, millets, legumes, oats, psyllium, fenugreek, bitter gourd, cinnamon, nuts, coffee and tea (associated with lower risk) |
| **Cancer** | Tomato (lycopene), cruciferous vegetables (sulforaphane, indoles), garlic and onion (organosulphur compounds), green tea (EGCG), turmeric (curcumin), soy (isoflavones), flaxseed (lignans), berries (anthocyanins, ellagic acid), whole-grain fibre, probiotic curd |
| **Obesity** | High-fibre foods, high-protein foods, green tea, low-energy-density foods |
| **Osteoporosis** | Calcium- and vitamin D-fortified milk and juices, soy isoflavones, green leafy vegetables (vitamin K), ragi |
| **Gut health and colon cancer** | Probiotic curd and drinks, prebiotic fibres (inulin), wheat bran |
| **Eye disease (cataract, AMD)** | Green leafy vegetables, egg yolk, maize (lutein, zeaxanthin), fish (DHA) |
| **Cognitive decline** | Fish (DHA), berries (anthocyanins), green tea, nuts |
| **Urinary tract infections** | Cranberry (proanthocyanidins that stop bacteria sticking) |

The overall message: a **varied diet** rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, pulses, nuts and fish, with probiotic foods, gives the widest range of protective compounds. Functional foods support, but do not replace, medical treatment and a healthy lifestyle.

## Remember

- Diabetes: glucose auto-oxidation, AGEs–RAGE, polyol pathway (uses NADPH), PKC; β-cells are low in catalase and GPx (alloxan, streptozotocin).
- Inflammation: respiratory burst (NADPH oxidase), HOCl (myeloperoxidase), peroxynitrite; NF-κB vicious circle.
- Ischaemia–reperfusion: hypoxanthine builds up and xanthine dehydrogenase becomes xanthine oxidase; on reperfusion O2 gives superoxide; allopurinol protects.
- Cancer: ROS cause DNA mutations (initiation), act as growth signals (promotion); many anticancer drugs work through ROS.
- Atherosclerosis: oxidised LDL → scavenger receptors → foam cells → fatty streak → plaque.
- Brain is vulnerable: high oxygen use, PUFAs, iron, low catalase, dopamine oxidation; Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, ALS (SOD1).
- Kidney: cisplatin, gentamicin, myoglobin; muscle: strenuous exercise, dystrophies.
- Free radical theory of ageing: Harman, 1956; lipofuscin, mitochondrial theory, caloric restriction; supplements have not extended lifespan.
- SOD: 2 O2•⁻ + 2H⁺ → H2O2 + O2 (Cu/Zn cytosol, Mn mitochondria); catalase: 2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2 (haem, peroxisomes); GPx: H2O2 + 2 GSH → GSSG + 2 H2O (selenium).
- Glutathione = γ-Glu-Cys-Gly; lipoic acid = network antioxidant (DHLA) and PDH cofactor; melatonin = pineal indoleamine, crosses BBB.
- BHT and BHA = hindered phenols, chain-breaking antioxidants for fats and oils; synergy with citric acid.
